name: Industrial
about: Industrial began in 1976 when Throbbing Gristle founded Industrial Records in Hackney and announced industrial music for industrial people: tape loops, found sound, cheap synthesizers and deliberately ugly subject matter, with no interest in rock's forms. Sheffield's Cabaret Voltaire, Berlin's Einstürzende Neubauten, who played scrap metal and power tools, and Australia's SPK made it a transnational movement, and Coil, Nurse With Wound and Test Dept carried its occult, collage and agitprop strands through the 1980s. In Chicago and Vancouver it hardened into the beat-driven electro-industrial of Ministry and Skinny Puppy, Godflesh fused it with metal in Birmingham, and Nine Inch Nails took the whole idea to arenas in the 1990s. The lineage runs on today in power electronics and the harsh, confrontational work of Pharmakon and Prurient.

artists.name: Throbbing Gristle
artists.why: coined the term and defined the sound

artists.name: Coil
artists.why: occult electronics of Balance and Christopherson

albums.title: The Second Annual Report
albums.why: Live tapes and the Slug Bait and Maggot Death pieces, pressed in an edition of 785, mark the moment industrial music was named and demonstrated.

albums.title: 20 Jazz Funk Greats
albums.why: Beneath the suicide-cliff sleeve and a title that is a joke, TG wrote proto-techno, exotica and dread into one album that every later electronic deviant studied.

albums.title: Mix-Up
albums.why: The Sheffield trio's first album cuts tape loops, treated vocals and a garage-band stomp into something that was neither punk nor electronic pop but both.

albums.title: Chance Meeting on a Dissecting Table of a Sewing Machine and an Umbrella
albums.why: A surrealist improvisation famous as much for the list of obscure records on its sleeve as for its music; uneven, but a founding text of the British underground.

albums.title: Red Mecca
albums.why: Dub basslines, treated guitar and a sustained paranoid mood make this the Cabs' most complete album and a bridge from industrial to the dance floor.

albums.title: Kollaps
albums.why: Drills, sheet metal and Blixa Bargeld's shriek on a debut that treated West Berlin's ruins as an instrument; close to unlistenable then, historic now.

albums.title: Leichenschrei
albums.why: Clinical samples, pounding percussion and medical horror from Sydney, often cited as the most extreme and fully realised of the first-wave industrial albums.

albums.title: Dreams Less Sweet
albums.why: Genesis P-Orridge's post-TG project at its most ambitious, with choirs, Tibetan thighbone trumpets and holophonic recording on a strange, lavish record.

albums.title: Cop
albums.why: Michael Gira's early Swans at their slowest and most punishing, a document of New York's industrial-noise scene that still sounds like a beating.

albums.title: Beating the Retreat
albums.why: Metal-bashing percussion and Soviet-constructivist fervour from a south London collective who took their music into the miners' strike.

albums.title: Nail
albums.why: J.G. Thirlwell's big-band-from-hell approach peaks here, with orchestral samples, swing rhythms and self-loathing lyrics delivered as cabaret.

albums.title: Halber Mensch
albums.why: The album where Neubauten became composers rather than demolitionists, its a cappella title track and controlled percussion the peak of their first decade.

albums.title: Horse Rotorvator
albums.why: Death, AIDS-era London and Pasolini run through Coil's second album, which moves from brass fanfares to Ostia's elegy with rare compositional grace.

albums.title: Opus Dei
albums.why: The Slovenian collective's martial covers of Life Is Life and One Vision made their totalitarian-pop satire famous, and the originals around them hold up.

albums.title: Front by Front
albums.why: Headhunter and Welcome to Paradise define electronic body music: sequenced, muscular and clubbable, the Belgian group's best and most influential set.

albums.title: The Land of Rape and Honey
albums.why: Al Jourgensen abandoned synth-pop for sampled riffs, metal guitars and relentless drum programming, and the industrial-metal template was set.

albums.title: Pretty Hate Machine
albums.why: Trent Reznor turned the Chicago and Vancouver sound into pop songs about hurt and control, and a genre of basement cassettes suddenly sold a million.

albums.title: Streetcleaner
albums.why: Drum machine, down-tuned guitar and Justin Broadrick's bellow from Birmingham on the record that invented industrial metal and still sounds heavier than its successors.

albums.title: Too Dark Park
albums.why: Layered samples, Ogre's distorted vocals and an ecological-apocalypse theme on the Vancouver trio's densest and most carefully produced album.

albums.title: Love's Secret Domain
albums.why: Coil's acid-house record, where the occult and the dance floor meet in Windowpane and the title track, and the genre's most sensual album.

albums.title: The Downward Spiral
albums.why: A concept album about self-destruction recorded in the Tate house, it carried industrial textures and real songwriting to the top of the charts without compromise.

albums.title: Bestial Burden
albums.why: Written after an emergency surgery, Margaret Chardiet's second album turns the body's failure into power electronics of unusual focus and physical force.

albums.title: Frozen Niagara Falls
albums.why: Dominick Fernow's double album ranges from harsh noise to acoustic guitar and spoken confession, the most ambitious record of the post-2000 noise underground.

albums.title: Caligula
albums.why: Kristin Hayter sets survivor's rage to operatic voice, piano and industrial roar, an album that extended the genre's confrontational tradition into new territory.
